en: gangjeong; traditional Korean sweet grain snack

examples.en: My grandmother made gangjeong for the holiday.

examples.ko: 이 강정은 너무 달지 않아서 좋아요.
examples.en: I like this gangjeong because it isn't too sweet.

examples.ko: 시장에서 맛있는 강정을 한 봉지 샀어요.
examples.en: I bought a bag of tasty gangjeong at the market.
Do you have any gangjeong to eat with tea?
I wrapped the gift box of gangjeong nicely.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 먹던 강정 맛이 아직도 생각나요.
examples.en: I still remember the taste of the gangjeong I ate as a child.

explain: '닭강정'은 달콤매콤한 소스를 입힌 닭튀김이라서 전통 과자 강정과 달라요. 이름은 같아도 가게에서 '강정'만 말하면 보통 명절 과자를 떠올려요.
explain_en: '닭강정' is sweet-spicy fried chicken, a different food from the traditional snack. If you just say '강정' alone, most people think of the holiday snack.

examples.en: There is less oxygen at high altitude, so I get out of breath.
Winter comes early in the highlands.

examples.ko: 그 마을은 고산에 있어서 길이 가팔라요.
examples.en: That village is high in the mountains, so the roads are steep.
Alpine plants withstand the cold well.
I had a headache because of altitude sickness.

examples.ko: 해발 삼천 미터가 넘는 고산을 오르는 게 꿈이에요.
examples.en: My dream is to climb a high mountain over three thousand meters.

explain: '고산'은 '고산병', '고산 식물', '고산 지대'처럼 다른 말과 합쳐서 자주 써요. 산 하나를 가리킬 때는 그냥 '산'이나 '높은 산'이라고 해요.
explain_en: '고산' is mostly used in compounds like '고산병', '고산 식물' and '고산 지대'. To point to a single mountain, people just say '산' or '높은 산'.

examples.en: The lights went out, so the room is pitch dark.
I walked alone down the pitch-dark road at night.
In the dark, only the phone light was on.
It's only six in the evening and it's already dark.
When I close my eyes, everything goes black.
Thinking about the test result made me feel hopeless.

explain: 보통 '깜깜하다'로 써요. '캄캄하다'도 같은 말인데 '깜깜하다'가 더 센 느낌이에요. 소식을 전혀 모를 때 '깜깜무소식'이라고도 해요.

phrases.en: to feel hopeless about the future
phrases.nuance_ko: 어떻게 해야 할지 몰라 막막할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used when you have no idea what to do and the future looks bleak.

explain_en: It is usually used as '깜깜하다'. '캄캄하다' means the same, but '깜깜하다' feels stronger. When you hear nothing at all, people say '깜깜무소식'.

en: be optimistic; take an optimistic view

examples.ko: 저는 이번 일이 잘될 거라고 낙관해요.
examples.en: I'm optimistic that this will go well.
Experts aren't optimistic about an economic recovery.
I was too optimistic and made a big mistake.
It's still too early to be optimistic about the result.
He is someone who takes an optimistic view of the future.
It's a situation where we still can't be optimistic.

explain: 반대말은 '비관하다'예요. 뉴스나 회사에서는 '낙관적이다', '낙관할 수 없다'를 자주 들어요. 일상 대화에서는 '잘될 거예요', '긍정적이에요'를 더 많이 말해요.
explain_en: The opposite is '비관하다'. In news and at work you often hear '낙관적이다' and '낙관할 수 없다'. In everyday talk people more often say '잘될 거예요' or '긍정적이에요'.

examples.ko: 친구들의 놀림 때문에 학교 가기 싫었어요.
examples.en: I didn't want to go to school because my friends teased me.
I got teased because of my nickname.

examples.ko: 그 아이는 놀림거리가 되는 게 싫대요.
examples.en: I heard that kid hates being the butt of jokes.
Don't get angry at the teasing, just laugh it off.
I was teased for being short when I was little.
The joking went too far and turned into teasing.

explain: '놀림을 받다', '놀림을 당하다'로 자주 써요. 친한 사이의 '장난'과 달리 '놀림'은 듣는 사람이 기분이 나쁠 때 써요. 하는 쪽은 '놀리다'라고 해요.
explain_en: It is often used as '놀림을 받다' or '놀림을 당하다'. Unlike '장난' between close friends, '놀림' is used when the other person feels hurt. The person doing it is said to '놀리다'.

examples.en: I studied Korean on my own.
Self-study was hard, so I signed up for an academy.
Many people teach themselves guitar.
I'm teaching myself by watching videos.
Since you study alone, a plan is important in self-study.
He taught himself and passed the exam.

explain: '독학하다'로도 쓰고 '독학으로'를 자주 써요. 학원이나 선생님 없이 혼자 배우는 일이라서 '혼자 공부하다'보다 목표가 분명한 느낌이에요. '자습'은 학교나 학원에서 스스로 공부하는 시간을 말해요.
explain_en: It is used as '독학하다' and very often as '독학으로'. It means learning without a teacher or academy, with a clearer goal than '혼자 공부하다'. '자습' is the self-study time inside a school or academy.

examples.en: The US is a long-time ally of Korea.
The two countries decided to become allies.
The allied nations gathered in one place.
We received help from an ally during the war.

examples.ko: 동맹국 사이에도 의견이 다를 수 있어요.
examples.en: Even allies can have different opinions.

examples.ko: 그 나라는 우리의 가장 가까운 동맹국 중 하나예요.
examples.en: That country is one of our closest allies.

explain: '동맹을 맺다'처럼 '동맹'은 서로 돕기로 약속하는 관계고, '동맹국'은 그 약속을 한 나라예요. '우방국'은 사이가 좋은 나라를 말하고, '동맹국'은 약속이 공식적인 나라라는 차이가 있어요.
explain_en: '동맹' is the pact itself, as in '동맹을 맺다', and '동맹국' is a country in that pact. '우방국' is a friendly country, while '동맹국' has a formal agreement.

examples.en: That child is young but really bright.
A sharp junior joined, so I feel reassured.
It was a child with bright-looking eyes.
I'm raising a smart-looking puppy.

examples.ko: 우리 딸은 똘똘해서 말을 빨리 배웠어요.
examples.en: My daughter is bright and learned to talk early.
Class is fun thanks to a bright student.

explain: 주로 어린아이나 젊은 사람을 칭찬할 때 써요. 어른에게 쓰면 아랫사람을 보는 느낌이 들 수 있어서 '똑똑하다'가 더 안전해요. '똑똑하다'보다 야무지고 귀여운 느낌이에요.
explain_en: It is mainly used to praise children or young people. Used on an adult it can sound condescending, so '똑똑하다' is safer. It feels more sharp-and-cute than '똑똑하다'.

examples.en: This year's birthday was a meaningful time.
The trip with my family was meaningful.
Thank you for the meaningful gift.
This occasion means a lot to us.
Volunteering was a really meaningful experience.
The graduation ceremony ended in a meaningful way.

explain: '의미 있다'와 비슷하지만 '뜻깊다'는 마음에 오래 남는 일에 써요. '뜻깊은 시간/하루/경험'처럼 뒤에 명사를 붙여 많이 말해요. '의미 있는'은 중요하다는 쪽, '뜻깊은'은 소중하고 감동적이라는 쪽이에요.
explain_en: It is close to '의미 있다', but '뜻깊다' is for things that stay in your heart. It is often followed by a noun, as in '뜻깊은 시간', '뜻깊은 하루' and '뜻깊은 경험'. '의미 있는' leans toward important, while '뜻깊은' leans toward precious and moving.

examples.en: I tripped on the threshold and almost fell.
The baby couldn't get over the threshold and cried.
The sill is high, so wheelchairs can't get in.
Please take off your shoes before the threshold.
He sat on the threshold and tied his shoelaces.
It feels like we've stepped onto the edge of winter.

explain: '턱'은 계단이나 길의 높이 차이를 넓게 가리키고, '문턱'은 문 바로 아래에만 써요. '문턱을 넘다'는 어떤 단계에 처음 들어선다는 뜻으로도 써요.

phrases.example: 그 병원은 문턱이 높아서 가기 어려워요.
phrases.en: hard to get into; intimidating to approach
phrases.nuance_ko: 가게나 기관에 들어가거나 이용하기가 부담스러울 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used when a place or institution feels hard or intimidating to enter or use.

explain_en: '턱' is any small step in height on a path or stairs, while '문턱' is only the one right under a door. '문턱을 넘다' can also mean stepping into a new stage.

examples.en: Birds built a nest up in the tree.
My spouse and I set up a small, cozy home.
I made a warm nest for the cat.
We found our newlywed home in Seoul.

examples.ko: 이 집은 우리 가족의 소중한 보금자리예요.
examples.en: This house is our family's precious home.
The abandoned dogs found a new home.

explain: '집'보다 따뜻하고 포근한 느낌이 있어서 글이나 광고에서 자주 보여요. 새나 동물의 둥지에도 쓰고, '신혼 보금자리', '새 보금자리'처럼 새로 시작하는 곳에 많이 써요.
explain_en: It feels warmer and cozier than '집', so you often see it in writing and ads. It also works for the nests of birds and animals, and is common in phrases for a fresh start such as '신혼 보금자리' and '새 보금자리'.

examples.en: Please give me one copy of the contract.
I'll keep the original and give you just a copy.
I made a copy of the file and edited it.
I need a copy of the passport.
This copy is as clear as the original.
Don't stamp the copy.

explain: 반대말은 '원본'이에요. 종이를 복사기로 뽑은 것도, 컴퓨터 파일을 복제한 것도 '복사본'이라고 해요. 서류를 낼 때는 '사본'이라는 말도 같은 뜻으로 써요.
explain_en: The opposite is '원본'. Both a photocopy and a duplicated computer file are called '복사본'. When submitting documents, '사본' is also used with the same meaning.

examples.ko: 대학 때문에 열여덟 살에 서울로 상경했어요.
examples.en: I moved up to Seoul at eighteen for university.
My father went up to Seoul to find a job.

examples.ko: 시골에서 상경한 지 벌써 십 년이에요.
examples.en: It's already been ten years since I came up from the countryside.
I'm going up to Seoul briefly tomorrow for some documents.
Be sure to contact me when you come up to Seoul.
He went up to Seoul carrying his dream.

explain: 지방에서 서울로 올라갈 때만 써요. 말할 때는 '올라가다'가 더 자연스럽고, 반대로 지방으로 갈 때는 '내려가다'라고 해요. '서울로 상경하다'는 뜻이 겹친다고 보는 사람도 있지만 많이 써요.
explain_en: It is only used for going from the provinces to Seoul. In speech '올라가다' sounds more natural, and going the other way is '내려가다'. Some people say '서울로 상경하다' is redundant, but it is common.

en: birthplace house; childhood home of a famous person

examples.en: We visited the poet's birthplace.
The birthplace house was turned into a museum.

examples.ko: 그분의 생가는 작은 시골 마을에 있어요.
examples.en: His birthplace is in a small country village.
On the weekend I took photos in front of the birthplace.
The restoration work on the birthplace is finished.
I'm touring the birthplace of a famous painter.

explain: 유명한 사람이 태어난 집에 쓰는 말이라서 보통 사람에게는 잘 안 써요. 평범한 사람이 태어나 자란 집은 '고향집'이라고 해요. 박물관이나 관광지 안내에서 '생가'를 자주 봐요.
explain_en: It is used for the house where a famous person was born, so it is rarely used for ordinary people. The house an ordinary person grew up in is called '고향집'. You often see '생가' on museum and tourist signs.

examples.ko: 오늘은 여느 날과 다르게 일찍 일어났어요.
examples.en: Today I woke up early, unlike any usual day.
I had coffee and went to work as usual.

examples.ko: 그 집 음식은 여느 식당보다 맛있어요.
examples.en: That place's food tastes better than at an ordinary restaurant.
Like any other kid, he likes comics.
This winter is colder than an average year.
That day started just like any other weekend.

explain: '여느'는 항상 뒤에 명사가 와요. '여느 때/날/사람'처럼 쓰고 보통 '~와 다르다', '~처럼', '~보다'가 따라와요. '다른'은 서로 같지 않다는 뜻이고 '여느'는 '평범한'이라는 뜻이라 헷갈리지 않게 주의하세요.
explain_en: '여느' must always be followed by a noun, as in '여느 때', '여느 날' and '여느 사람', and is usually followed by '~와 다르다', '~처럼' or '~보다'. '다른' means not the same, but '여느' means ordinary, so be careful not to mix them up.

examples.en: My father went to reserve forces training today.
A man who has finished the army becomes a reservist.
I took a day off because of reserve training.
People in reserve-forces uniforms got on the bus.

examples.ko: 동네 예비군 부대가 학교 옆에 있어요.
examples.en: The local reserve forces unit is next to the school.

examples.ko: 예비군은 몇 년 동안 훈련을 받아요.
examples.en: Reservists receive training for several years.

explain: 군대를 마친 한국 남자가 일정 기간 받는 훈련을 '예비군 훈련'이라고 해요. 남자들이 '예비군 간다'처럼 아주 일상적으로 말해요. 여자는 대상이 아니라서 친구나 아버지 이야기에 주로 나와요.
explain_en: Korean men who have finished the army must attend '예비군 훈련' for a set period. Men casually say '예비군 간다' for it. Women are not subject to it, so it mostly comes up in talk about a friend or father.

examples.en: The number of subway users is growing every year.
There are many park visitors on weekends.
The users are lining up and waiting.
A bus for airport users has started running.
They added seats to reduce inconvenience for users.
Ski resort visitors increase in winter.

explain: 버스, 지하철, 공항, 도서관처럼 시설이나 교통을 쓰는 사람에게 써요. '손님'은 가게에서 쓰고, '승객'은 탈것에 탄 사람만 가리켜서 범위가 더 좁아요. 안내문이나 뉴스에서 자주 나와요.
explain_en: It refers to people who use a facility or transport such as a bus, subway, airport or library. '손님' is used in shops, and '승객' only covers people riding a vehicle, so it is narrower. It appears often in notices and news.

examples.ko: 그녀는 유명한 저널리스트가 되고 싶어 해요.
examples.en: She wants to become a famous journalist.
A journalist is taking photos at the scene.
A journalist has to check the facts accurately.
My uncle worked as a journalist for a long time.
I set up an interview with a journalist.
I read a book by a journalist working abroad.

explain: '기자'가 훨씬 흔해요. '저널리스트'는 신문사 소속이 아니어도 글이나 영상으로 취재하는 사람까지 넓게 가리키고, 조금 전문적이고 멋진 느낌이 있어요. 신문사나 방송국에서 일하는 사람은 보통 '기자'라고 불러요.
explain_en: '기자' is far more common. '저널리스트' can also cover people who report through writing or video without belonging to a newspaper, and it sounds a bit more professional and stylish. People working at a newspaper or broadcaster are usually called '기자'.

examples.en: Milk should be stored at a low temperature.
I put the fruit in a cold storage room.
Low-temperature burns happen without you noticing.
You bake this dish slowly at a low temperature.
Batteries drain quickly in low temperatures.
I bought low-temperature pasteurized milk.

explain: 반대말은 '고온'이에요. 날씨는 '춥다', '쌀쌀하다'로 말하고, '저온'은 보관·요리·과학처럼 온도를 따질 때 주로 써요. '저온 보관', '저온 창고', '저온 화상'처럼 합쳐서 자주 나와요.
explain_en: The opposite is '고온'. For weather people say '춥다' or '쌀쌀하다', and '저온' is mainly used when temperature matters, as in storage, cooking and science. It often appears in compounds like '저온 보관', '저온 창고' and '저온 화상'.

examples.en: I glued the broken cup back together.
The glue got on my hand and won't come off.
This adhesive sticks well to wood.
Don't apply too much glue.
You have to wait until the glue dries.
I bought a strong adhesive at the store.

explain: 일상에서는 '풀'과 '본드'를 더 많이 말해요. '풀'은 종이에, '본드'는 나무나 플라스틱 같은 단단한 것에 쓰는 접착제예요. 가게에서 '접착제'라고 해도 다 알아들어요.
explain_en: In daily life people say '풀' and '본드' more often. '풀' is for paper and '본드' is for hard things like wood or plastic. Saying '접착제' at a store is understood by everyone.

examples.en: I learn singing at a neighborhood chorus group.

examples.ko: 코러스 팀이 무대 뒤에서 화음을 넣었어요.
examples.en: The backing singers added harmony from behind the stage.
We practiced chorus singing in music class.
Church chorus practice is every Saturday.
The backing vocals in this song are really great.
He started as a backing singer and became a singer.

explain: '합창'은 여러 사람이 함께 부르는 노래이고, '코러스'는 가수 뒤에서 화음을 넣는 사람이나 그 소리를 말할 때 많이 써요. 노래에서 반복되는 부분은 '코러스'가 아니라 '후렴'이라고 해요.
explain_en: '합창' is a song sung together by many people, while '코러스' is more often used for the people who sing harmony behind a singer, or that sound. The repeated part of a song is called '후렴', not '코러스'.

examples.en: A panorama of the city spread out from the observatory.
I took a panorama photo with my phone.

examples.ko: 산 정상에서 본 파노라마가 정말 멋졌어요.
examples.en: The panorama from the summit was really beautiful.

examples.ko: 파노라마 창문 덕분에 바다가 다 보여요.
examples.en: Thanks to the panoramic window, I can see the whole sea.
I previewed the destination in a panoramic video.

examples.ko: 카페에서 한강 파노라마를 볼 수 있어요.
examples.en: You can see a panorama of the Han River from the cafe.

explain: 카메라 기능으로는 '파노라마 모드'가 가장 흔해요. 풍경을 말할 때는 '탁 트인 전망'과 비슷하고, '지난 일이 파노라마처럼 스쳐 가다'처럼 기억이 연달아 떠오를 때도 써요.
explain_en: On a camera, '파노라마 모드' is the most common use. For scenery it is close to a wide open view, and it is also used when memories pass by one after another, as in '지난 일이 파노라마처럼 스쳐 가다'.

examples.ko: 쌀 한 포대를 사서 집에 가져왔어요.
examples.en: I bought a sack of rice and brought it home.
I filled the sack with potatoes.
The cement sack is too heavy for me to lift.

examples.ko: 할머니가 고구마 한 포대를 보내 주셨어요.
examples.en: My grandmother sent me a sack of sweet potatoes.
I tied the sacks and stacked them in the warehouse.
The flour sack tore and the floor turned white.

explain: '한 포대, 두 포대'처럼 큰 자루를 세는 단위로도 많이 써요. '자루'는 크기에 상관없이 쓰고, 작은 것은 '봉지'라고 해요. '쌀 한 포대'처럼 무겁고 많은 양을 말할 때 잘 어울려요.
explain_en: It is also widely used as a counter for large sacks, as in '한 포대, 두 포대'. '자루' is used regardless of size, and small ones are '봉지'. It fits heavy, large amounts, as in '쌀 한 포대'.

examples.en: Let's not waste time and start now.
I wasted the morning looking at my phone.
I regretted it after squandering the money.
He is wasting his talent.
I feel like I wasted a precious day.
I turned off the light so as not to waste energy.

explain: '시간, 돈, 재능, 에너지'처럼 아까운 것을 쓸모없게 쓸 때 써요. '낭비하다'와 거의 같지만 '시간을 허비하다'가 훨씬 자연스럽고, 돈에는 '낭비하다'를 더 많이 써요. 반대로 쓸모 있게 쓰는 건 '활용하다', '아끼다'예요.
explain_en: It is used when something precious such as '시간', '돈', '재능' or '에너지' is spent for nothing. It is nearly the same as '낭비하다', but '시간을 허비하다' sounds much more natural, while '낭비하다' is more common for money. Using things well is '활용하다' or '아끼다'.

examples.ko: 이 땅은 오랫동안 황무지로 남아 있었어요.
examples.en: This land remained a wasteland for a long time.
They began planting trees on the barren land.
He turned the wasteland into a field.
There was only wind on the wasteland, and nothing else.
The village everyone left became a wasteland.
We started over in a place like a wasteland.

explain: 농사를 짓지 않고 버려 둔 거친 땅에 써요. '황무지에서 꽃을 피우다'처럼 아무것도 없는 곳에서 성과를 낸다는 비유로도 자주 써요. '사막'은 모래와 건조한 기후 때문에 생긴 땅이라 다른 말이에요.
explain_en: It is used for rough land left unfarmed. It is also often used figuratively, as in '황무지에서 꽃을 피우다', for achieving something where there was nothing. '사막' is land formed by sand and a dry climate, so it is a different word.

examples.en: He whistled because he was in a good mood.
A whistling sound echoes in the alley.

examples.ko: 밤에 휘파람을 불면 안 된다고 해요.
examples.en: They say you shouldn't whistle at night.
My friend sent a signal by whistling.
Please teach me how to whistle.
The puppy ran over at the sound of the whistle.

explain: '휘파람을 불다'로 짝지어 써요. '노래를 부르다'의 '부르다'가 아니라 '불다'라서 헷갈리지 않게 주의하세요. 한국에는 '밤에 휘파람을 불면 뱀이 나온다'는 옛말이 있어요.
explain_en: It pairs with the verb '불다' as in '휘파람을 불다'. It is '불다', not the '부르다' of '노래를 부르다', so watch out for mixing them up. Korea has an old saying, '밤에 휘파람을 불면 뱀이 나온다'.

examples.en: The child suffered from a high fever all night.
I had a high fever, so I went to the hospital.
I couldn't go to school because of a high fever.
The high fever hasn't gone down for three days.

examples.ko: 고열과 기침이 같이 오면 검사를 받으세요.
examples.en: If you get a high fever along with a cough, get tested.

examples.ko: 고열 환자는 물을 많이 마셔야 해요.
examples.en: A patient with a high fever must drink a lot of water.

explain: 일상에서는 '열이 많이 나다'라고 말하고, '고열'은 병원이나 뉴스처럼 좀 더 정확하게 말할 때 써요. 가벼운 열은 '미열'이라고 해요. '고열이 나다', '고열에 시달리다'로 자주 말해요.
explain_en: In daily life people say '열이 많이 나다', and '고열' is used in hospitals and news where the speech is more precise. A slight fever is '미열'. It is often used as '고열이 나다' or '고열에 시달리다'.

examples.en: That professor is a well-known eccentric.
My eccentric friend made a strange invention.
He seems like an oddball, but he's actually kind.

examples.ko: 우리 반에는 괴짜가 한 명 있어요.
examples.en: There is one oddball in our class.
I watched a movie about an eccentric genius.

examples.ko: 괴짜라는 말을 듣는 게 싫지 않아요.
examples.en: I don't mind being called an oddball.

explain: 조금 별나지만 재미있거나 재능 있는 사람에게 써서 나쁜 뜻만 있는 말은 아니에요. '이상한 사람'은 기분 나쁘게 들릴 수 있어서 가까운 사이가 아니면 '독특하다'가 더 부드러워요. 사람에게만 써요.
explain_en: It is used for someone a bit odd but fun or talented, so it is not purely negative. '이상한 사람' can sound rude, so unless you are close, '독특하다' is softer. It is used only for people.

examples.en: A big hole appeared in the road.
I fell into a hole and my shoes got wet.
I dug a hole to plant a tree.

examples.ko: 공사 때문에 구덩이 앞에 표지판을 세웠어요.
examples.en: They put up a sign in front of the pit because of construction.
When it rains, water collects in the pit.
The child is playing in a sand pit.

explain: '구덩이를 파다'처럼 '파다'와 짝지어 써요. '웅덩이'는 물이 고인 곳이고 '구덩이'는 물이 없어도 써요. 땅이 푹 꺼진 곳에 쓰고, 벽에 난 작은 구멍에는 '구멍'을 써요.
explain_en: It pairs with '파다', as in '구덩이를 파다'. '웅덩이' is a hollow with water in it, while '구덩이' can be dry. It is for a dip in the ground; a small hole in a wall is '구멍'.

examples.en: I gave every student an equal chance.
Please divide the cake evenly.
Incomes are not equal, so the problem is big.
Equal educational opportunity is important.
The three of us paid the cost evenly.
Rain falls evenly across that area.

explain: '균등하게'로 가장 많이 쓰고, 기회·권리·분배 같은 제도 이야기에 잘 어울려요. 일상에서 같은 양으로 나눌 때는 '똑같이', '공평하게'를 더 많이 써요. '공평하다'는 치우치지 않는 느낌이고 '균등하다'는 양이 같은 느낌이에요.
explain_en: It is most often used as '균등하게' and fits talk about systems such as opportunity, rights and distribution. In daily life, splitting equally is usually '똑같이' or '공평하게'. '공평하다' feels unbiased, while '균등하다' feels equal in amount.

examples.en: That student won the gold prize at the contest.
The gold prize work is hanging in the lobby.
I'm happy that our team won the gold prize.
They announce the gold, silver, and bronze prizes in that order.
The gold prize winner gave a speech.
I took the gold prize in a drawing contest.

explain: 한국 대회에서는 '대상, 금상, 은상, 동상'으로 상을 나누는 경우가 많아요. '대상'이 있으면 '대상'이 가장 높고, '대상'이 없으면 '금상'이 가장 높아서 대회마다 순위가 달라요.
explain_en: Korean contests often split prizes into '대상', '금상', '은상' and '동상'. If there is a '대상' it is the top one, and if there isn't, '금상' is the top, so the ranking depends on the contest.

examples.en: The family gathers to make winter kimchi.
This weekend we made winter kimchi at Grandma's house.

examples.ko: 올해는 배추 오십 포기로 김장할 거예요.
examples.en: This year I'll make winter kimchi with fifty heads of cabbage.
On kimjang day, we eat boiled pork.

examples.ko: 요즘은 김장하지 않고 사 먹는 집도 많아요.
examples.en: These days many households buy kimchi instead of making it.

examples.ko: 어머니와 같이 김장하는 게 힘들지만 즐거워요.
examples.en: Making winter kimchi with my mother is tiring but fun.

explain: 그냥 김치를 담글 때는 '김치를 담그다'라고 하고, 늦가을에 겨울 동안 먹을 김치를 한꺼번에 많이 담글 때만 '김장하다'라고 해요. 이웃과 나눠 먹는 한국의 김장 문화는 유네스코 무형유산이에요.
explain_en: Making ordinary kimchi is '김치를 담그다'; '김장하다' is only for making a large batch in late autumn to last the winter. Korea's kimjang culture of sharing with neighbors is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

examples.en: I wash fruit that has been sprayed with pesticide thoroughly.
The farmer is spraying pesticide on the field.
I bought vegetables grown without pesticide.
They say bees are decreasing because of pesticides.
The pesticide smell was strong, so I closed the window.
I visited a farm that doesn't use pesticides.

explain: '농약을 치다', '농약을 뿌리다'처럼 말하고, 마트에서는 '무농약', '저농약' 표시를 볼 수 있어요. 벌레를 없애는 약은 '살충제', 풀을 없애는 약은 '제초제'라고 해요.
explain_en: People say '농약을 치다' or '농약을 뿌리다', and in supermarkets you will see labels like '무농약' and '저농약'. Medicine to kill insects is '살충제' and to kill weeds is '제초제'.

examples.en: I divided the dough into lumps and baked them.
I packed the snow into one lump.
I put a chunk of meat in the fridge.
I made a doll out of a lump of clay.
I broke the lump of soil with my hands.
The rice clumped together and tastes bad.

explain: '덩이'는 혼자 쓰기보다 '고깃덩이', '눈덩이', '흙덩이'처럼 다른 말 뒤에 붙는 경우가 많아요. 또 '한 덩이, 두 덩이'처럼 덩어리를 세는 단위로 써요. 비슷한 '덩어리'가 일상에서 더 흔해요.
explain_en: '덩이' is more often attached to another word, as in '고깃덩이', '눈덩이' and '흙덩이', than used alone. It is also a counter for lumps, as in '한 덩이, 두 덩이'. The similar '덩어리' is more common in daily speech.

examples.en: My cold was bad, so I got an IV drip.
I fell asleep while getting the IV drip.

examples.ko: 링거 바늘을 꽂을 때 아파서 얼굴을 찡그렸어요.
examples.en: It hurt when the IV needle went in, so I frowned.
The IV bottle is almost empty.
After getting the drip, I felt energized.
The nurse swapped in a new IV bag.

explain: '링거를 맞다'라고 하고 '먹다'를 쓰지 않아요. 원래는 수액의 한 종류 이름인데 한국에서는 팔에 꽂는 수액 주사를 통틀어 '링거'라고 해요. 병원에서 쓰는 정확한 말은 '수액'이에요.
explain_en: You say '링거를 맞다', never '먹다'. It was originally the name of one type of IV fluid, but in Korea '링거' covers any IV drip into the arm. The more exact hospital term is '수액'.

examples.en: A headband is convenient when you exercise.

examples.ko: 딸이 분홍색 머리띠를 사 달라고 했어요.
examples.en: My daughter asked me to buy her a pink headband.
My head hurts because of the headband.
I bought a cute headband at the festival.
With a headband on, my bangs don't fall down.
He tied a white band around his forehead.

explain: '머리띠를 하다'가 가장 자연스럽고 '두르다'도 써요. '머리핀'은 머리카락을 고정하는 작은 물건이고, '머리띠'는 머리 둘레를 감는 것이에요. 시험 응원 때 이마에 두르는 천도 '머리띠'라고 해요.
explain_en: '머리띠를 하다' is the most natural, and '두르다' also works. A '머리핀' is a small clip that holds hair, while a '머리띠' wraps around the head. The cloth tied on the forehead to cheer for an exam is also a '머리띠'.

examples.en: Careless driving leads to accidents.
I was careless and broke a cup.
I opened the door carelessly and hurt my hand.
He is sometimes careless with his words.
I lost points because of a careless mistake.

examples.ko: 약을 부주의하게 두면 아이가 먹을 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you leave medicine carelessly, a child could eat it.

explain: 반대말은 '조심하다', '주의하다'예요. '부주의하다'는 안전 안내문이나 사고 뉴스에서 자주 보이고, 사람에게 직접 쓰면 비판하는 느낌이 강해요. 일상 대화에서는 '덜렁대다'나 '조심성이 없다'를 더 많이 써요.
explain_en: The opposites are '조심하다' and '주의하다'. '부주의하다' appears often in safety notices and accident news, and said directly to a person it sounds quite critical. In daily talk, '덜렁대다' or '조심성이 없다' are more common.

examples.ko: 산 입구에 오래된 비석이 서 있어요.
examples.en: An old stone monument stands at the mountain entrance.
A name is carved on the stone.
I laid flowers and paid my respects in front of the gravestone.

examples.ko: 이 마을에는 옛 장군의 비석이 있어요.
examples.en: This village has a stone monument for an old general.
The writing on the stone is worn and hard to read.

examples.ko: 학교 앞 비석에 학교의 역사가 적혀 있어요.
examples.en: The school's history is written on the monument in front of it.

explain: 무덤 앞의 돌은 '묘비', 사건이나 사람을 기념해 세운 돌은 '기념비'예요. '비석'은 이런 돌을 두루 가리키고 관광지 앞에서 자주 보여요. '표지석'은 장소를 알려 주는 돌이에요.
explain_en: A stone at a grave is a '묘비', and one set up to commemorate an event or person is a '기념비'. '비석' broadly covers these stones and is often seen at tourist spots. A '표지석' is a stone that marks a place.

examples.ko: 이 그림은 따뜻한 색조가 마음에 들어요.
examples.en: I like the warm tones of this painting.
I made the tone of the photo a bit darker.

examples.ko: 차분한 색조의 옷을 입고 면접을 봤어요.
examples.en: I wore clothes in calm tones to the interview.
I decorated the whole room in bright tones.
I went to the department store to buy color makeup.
The tones of the evening sky kept changing.

explain: '색깔'은 하나의 색, '색조'는 색들이 어울린 전체 분위기예요. 화장품 가게에서는 '색조 화장'이 립스틱·섀도처럼 색을 입히는 화장이라서 따로 알아 두세요.
explain_en: '색깔' is one color, while '색조' is the overall mood of colors working together. In a cosmetics shop, '색조 화장' means color makeup like lipstick and eyeshadow, so learn that separately.

en: chilling; creepy; frightened with a sudden chill

examples.en: A sudden sound on the night road gave me chills.
The last scene of that movie is chilling.
I got a creepy feeling and looked behind me.
I felt a chill after watching the news.
When a cold hand touched me, a chill ran down my back.
The creepily smiling doll is scary.

explain: '무섭다'보다 갑자기 소름이 끼치는 느낌이에요. 소리, 장면, 이야기에 대해 '섬뜩한 느낌/기분'이 든다고 자주 말해요. '오싹하다'는 추위나 공포에 몸이 떨리는 느낌이고, '섬뜩하다'는 마음이 서늘해지는 느낌이에요.
explain_en: It is the feeling of sudden goosebumps, more than plain '무섭다'. People often say '섬뜩한 느낌' or '섬뜩한 기분' about a sound, a scene or a story. '오싹하다' is a shudder from cold or fear in the body, while '섬뜩하다' is a chill in the mind.

en: end of a century; fin de siecle

examples.ko: 그 소설은 세기말의 불안한 분위기를 그려요.
examples.en: That novel depicts the anxious mood of the end of the century.

examples.ko: 세기말에는 새 시대에 대한 기대가 컸어요.
examples.en: At the turn of the century, expectations for a new era were high.

examples.ko: 사람들은 세기말이 오면 세상이 끝날까 걱정했어요.
examples.en: People worried the world might end when the century turned.

examples.ko: 세기말 감성의 음악이 요즘 다시 유행해요.
examples.en: Music with a turn-of-the-century vibe is trending again.
I watched a movie with an end-of-an-era atmosphere.
Turn-of-the-century fashion is popular again these days.

explain: 한 세기가 끝나 갈 때를 말하는데, 한국에서는 보통 2000년을 앞둔 1990년대 말을 떠올려요. '세기말 감성'은 그 시절의 불안하면서도 화려한 분위기를 가리켜요.
explain_en: It means the time when a century is ending, and in Korea people usually picture the late 1990s before the year 2000. '세기말 감성' refers to the anxious yet flashy mood of that era.

examples.en: I tried trout sashimi in Gangwon-do.
I went for a trout fishing experience.
Trout live in cold, clear water.
I caught a trout myself at the winter festival.
I squeezed lemon on the grilled trout and ate it.
My mother grilled a trout for me.

explain: 연어와 모양이 비슷하지만 송어는 주로 민물에서 길러 먹어요. 한국에서는 겨울 송어 축제와 '송어회'로 유명해요.
explain_en: It looks similar to salmon, but trout is mostly raised and eaten from fresh water. In Korea it is known for winter trout festivals and '송어회'.

en: undeniably; clearly; as a plain fact

examples.en: I am, without question, the owner of this house.
There are clearly rules, so please follow them.
That is undeniably illegal.

examples.ko: 엄연히 약속한 일인데 잊으면 안 돼요.
examples.en: We definitely promised, so you can't forget it.
Even though he's young, he is very much a member of the team.

examples.ko: 엄연히 주인이 있는 물건이니까 함부로 쓰면 안 돼요.
examples.en: This item clearly has an owner, so you can't just use it freely.

explain: 누가 모르는 척하거나 무시할 때 '분명한 사실이 있다'고 강하게 말하는 부사예요. 보통 '엄연히 ~이다', '엄연히 ~가 있다'로 쓰고, '분명히'와 뜻은 비슷한데 더 단호해요. 처음에는 '분명히'를 먼저 써도 돼요.
explain_en: This adverb is used when someone ignores or pretends not to know a fact, to say firmly that it clearly exists. It usually appears as '엄연히 ~이다' or '엄연히 ~가 있다', and is like '분명히' but more firm. At first it is fine to use '분명히' instead.

examples.ko: 작은 가게를 열 자본금을 모으고 있어요.
examples.en: I'm saving up the capital to open a small shop.

examples.ko: 회사를 만들 때 자본금이 얼마나 필요해요?
examples.en: How much capital do you need to start a company?
We didn't have enough capital, so we decided to take investment.
That company's capital is fifty million won.
I invested with a friend to increase the capital.
It's hard to start a business without capital.

explain: 가게를 열 때 쓰는 돈은 일상에서 '창업 자금'이나 '밑천'이라고 해요. 회사를 세울 때 법적으로 등록하는 돈일 때 '자본금'이라고 말해요.
explain_en: Everyday talk calls money for opening a shop '창업 자금' or '밑천'. '자본금' is used for the money legally registered when a company is founded.
